MedGuide AI combines accessible interaction, medical-source retrieval and explicit safety boundaries. The related work is therefore reviewed across retrieval-augmented generation, sentence embeddings, healthcare AI governance and local model execution. The literature motivates engineering choices; it does not establish the clinical validity of this project.

Lewis et al. [1] describe a generation architecture that combines a parametric language model with retrieved non-parametric knowledge. Their work demonstrates the value of retrieval for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks. For MedGuide, the relevant principle is that external evidence can be retrieved before an answer is generated, allowing the knowledge collection to be maintained separately from the model. The project adapts this principle to medical documents stored in PostgreSQL. Its evidence gate refuses a response when no acceptable chunk is retrieved. Retrieval can improve traceability, but it cannot guarantee that the retrieved passage is suitable for a particular patient or that every generated statement follows from the passage.

Sentence-BERT [2] uses sentence-level representations for semantic comparison and retrieval. MiniLM [3] studies transformer compression through attention distillation. These are relevant foundations for a compact embedding component. The model card for paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 [4] identifies a 384-dimensional sentence representation and multilingual support. MedGuide selects this identifier in knowledge_service.py and checks the resulting vector length. The model must be downloaded and loaded successfully; encoding failure is treated as unavailable evidence rather than replaced by invented vectors. General multilingual model support is not proof of reliable Hindi or Telugu medical retrieval; language-specific testing remains necessary.

WHO guidance on large multimodal models in health [5] discusses risks involving inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy and inappropriate reliance on AI. These considerations support MedGuide’s informational scope and professional-care boundary. The implementation includes refusal responses and deterministic checks before generation. Nevertheless, a rule list or prompt instruction is not a clinical safety certification. The project needs documented rule provenance, medical review and evaluation of false negatives, false positives and adversarial inputs before real patient use.

The repository includes four medical PDFs and a source register: WHO hypertension guidance, WHO PEN material, WHO malaria guidance and an ICMR paediatric/extrapulmonary tuberculosis workflow. The hypertension guideline [6] is a primary publication; the PEN package [7] concerns essential noncommunicable disease interventions. Such materials are knowledge inputs, not evidence that MedGuide is endorsed by their publishers. Page numbers, section text, publisher and source URL are retained with chunks. Publication version, licence and document review must remain traceable throughout ingestion.

The pgvector project [8] provides vector similarity search inside PostgreSQL. MedGuide uses its cosine-distance operator with 384-dimensional vectors, keeping source documents and chunks in the same relational system as application data. Ollama [9] provides a local model interface; its chat API accepts messages and returns generated content. MedGuide’s gateway supports Ollama, optional hosted inference and a mock provider. The configured Llama 3.2 3B candidate is an integration choice requiring hardware and language evaluation, not a final medically validated model.

The project targets the combination of rural accessibility, familiar-language interaction, visible evidence and a constrained informational role. The practical contribution is an integrated engineering prototype: a responsive interface, authenticated application routes, a relational care-data model and a retrieval/safety service boundary. Novel clinical performance, deployment effectiveness and user satisfaction have not been established. Comparisons with commercial symptom checkers or telemedicine platforms should be based on separately verified product evidence rather than assumptions about their language support, fees or capabilities.

The purpose is to provide an understandable first layer of healthcare information for rural and underserved communities. Distance, language and the difficulty of judging online information motivate a simple interface for asking questions, structuring symptoms and reviewing available evidence. The platform supports conversations with qualified healthcare professionals; it must not independently diagnose, prescribe or change treatment.

The engineering objective is to demonstrate how frontend design, REST APIs, authentication, relational storage, document processing, multilingual embeddings and local inference can be composed with explicit safety boundaries. Development uses synthetic information and an auditable source collection. The mini-project emphasises text interaction and preliminary symptom workflows rather than a claim of complete clinical deployment.

Laptop A is responsible for the server, database and AI infrastructure. Laptop B is responsible for user-facing interfaces. Both communicate through configurable API addresses. The separate mobile folder does not replace the Next.js website. Public website pages describe the product, while protected application screens support tasks. Extensive language expansion, autonomous decisions and real-world clinical deployment remain outside the approved mini-project boundary.

Requirements were organised around patient access, healthcare-worker involvement, safety, privacy and low digital literacy. Patient tasks include account access, symptom input, health questions, source inspection and review of personal information. Worker and administrative capabilities require role-based access and patient authorisation. Non-functional requirements include readable text, keyboard access, mobile touch targets, clear error states, low-bandwidth presentation and source traceability.

A feature is considered implemented only to the extent supported by its code and verification evidence. UI previews, registered API modules and evaluated clinical behaviour are different levels of completion. Acceptance checks therefore cover input validation, request handling, loading, refusal, errors, navigation and session isolation, rather than assuming that an attractive screen proves its backend service is available.

The web design uses warm cream surfaces, forest-green controls and restrained coral accents, with rural imagery in public pages. Reusable navigation, forms, device previews and informational components maintain visual consistency. The task-oriented workspace uses Home, Ask MedGuide and My information to reduce navigation burden. Separate mobile source code is intended to provide native layouts without altering the website.

FastAPI endpoints delegate work to services and receive SQLAlchemy sessions through dependencies. User accounts are associated with roles and patient profiles. Chat first resolves language and stores the patient message. A deterministic safety stage runs before retrieval. Routine queries are embedded, matched against approved documents and passed through an evidence gate. The local/optional/mock provider is hidden behind a gateway so the UI is not coupled to a model vendor.

PDF ingestion uses pypdf page extraction. The first non-empty line is treated as a baseline section label. Text is split into 500-character windows with 50-character overlap, not a sophisticated semantic segmentation algorithm. Metadata includes page, section, URL, publisher and embedding model. Empty pages are skipped; scanned-image pages would require OCR outside this implementation.

Software checks include frontend session tests, route/markup checks, API-contract tests and backend test modules for language resolution, retrieval, evidence refusal, output validation and provider errors. A report-time frontend run on 14 October 2026 completed 57 tests: 56 passed, none failed and one was skipped. This is a software regression result. The skipped case does not demonstrate live service behaviour. Backend README validation totals are historical development records, not tests rerun during this report preparation.

Clinical evaluation should use an approved reference set with expert-labelled expected escalation and evidence. Recommended measurements include retrieval recall at k, citation entailment, refusal appropriateness, false-negative rate, latency and language-specific error analysis. These are evaluation methods, not achieved results. Negation, hypothetical statements, spelling variation and code-switching require special attention in deterministic matching.

Local deployment starts PostgreSQL/pgvector and the API on Laptop A, with the Next.js interface on Laptop B. Environment configuration separates development URLs from application code. Database migrations must be applied before API use. Ollama generation requires a downloaded model and sufficient available memory. The repository inspected for this report does not supply a verified container deployment workflow; containerisation is therefore a deployment option rather than a completed result.

Maintenance includes reviewing medical source versions, preserving provenance, calibrating retrieval thresholds, checking dependency advisories and regression-testing safety behaviour. Rule changes require documented references and review. Future work includes validated speech and OCR services, careful medication review, authorised worker follow-up, measured mobile usability and explicit offline synchronisation. No claim of full offline operation, healthcare compliance certification or production readiness follows from the current prototype.

Laptop B needs a supported Node.js environment, a browser, source-control tools and enough disk space for frontend dependencies. Laptop A additionally needs Python, PostgreSQL with pgvector, model-cache storage and sufficient memory for the selected local model. A single fixed RAM minimum cannot guarantee LLM operation because model quantisation, context length and concurrent workloads affect memory. The backend README records a previous model generation failure due to insufficient available memory; hardware suitability must be checked on the actual machine.

These versions describe the inspected project snapshot, not a recommendation to ignore security updates. Dependency ranges in the backend are not a validated lockfile. 5.3.2 Installing Python and the FastAPI environment

Create an isolated Python virtual environment on Laptop A, install the repository requirements and copy backend/.env.example to backend/.env. Configure PostgreSQL credentials and a newly generated JWT secret. The environment file must never be committed. The following commands use a Unix shell; on Windows use the Scripts activation and executable paths.
Python installation commands are provided in the accompanying Word report.

Install PostgreSQL and the pgvector extension compatible with that installation [8]. Create an empty development database matching DATABASE_URL. Alembic applies the existing schema and vector extension; the database role needs the required extension permissions. Inspect migration completion separately from application liveness. A /api/v1/health response may be HTTP 200 while reporting database.status as disconnected.

Install Ollama from its official distribution [9]. The repository example selects AI_PROVIDER=ollama and AI_MODEL=llama3.2:3b. Run ollama pull llama3.2:3b on Laptop A and keep the local server available at OLLAMA_BASE_URL. Use AI_PROVIDER=mock for foundation testing. The model identifier is a candidate; successful download alone does not establish safe or accurate health guidance. The README’s previous llama3:latest inventory is not evidence that the 3B candidate has been evaluated.

HTTPX supplies provider requests, langdetect provides a language fallback, and Sentence Transformers loads the embedding model. Frontend libraries include React Aria, Motion and Lucide for interaction and accessibility. Medical PDF ingestion and model downloads are backend responsibilities. The separate Expo mobile prototype has its own package manifest and Node requirements; its dependencies must not be installed into the website.

The design separates presentation, API contracts, business services, persistence and AI providers. Public pages communicate the project’s purpose. Protected routes support patient tasks. The frontend client centralises URL configuration and token headers; real authentication request/response differences are mapped in that layer. Backend ownership checks tie conversations and symptom records to the authenticated patient, rather than trusting a patient identifier supplied by the browser.

The central router imports ten core modules. Speech and prescription-processing services are not registered there. Their interface references must not be counted as completed APIs. Request schemas, token verification and service ownership constraints must be reviewed together. UI route protection is only a presentation check; backend authorisation remains necessary.

The symptom service uses keyword matching while the chat service uses a separate regular-expression list. These lists are not identical and need a common reviewed specification. A lack of matches cannot rule out danger. The current output validator rejects out-of-range citation IDs and selected unsafe phrases, but it does not check entailment or require a citation in every answer. The evidence sufficiency test currently accepts any non-empty retrieved chunk list. These engineering limitations must be considered before making clinical claims.

    if not pdf_path.endswith(".pdf"):

    reader = PdfReader(pdf_path)
    extracted_pages = []

    for idx, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
        page_num = idx + 1
        text = page.extract_text() or ""
        text_clean = " ".join(text.split())
        if not text_clean:
            continue

        # Header detection baseline
        lines = [line.strip() for line in text.split("\n") if line.strip()]
        section_title = lines[0] if lines else f"Page {page_num}"

        extracted_pages.append({
            "page_number": page_num,
            "section_title": section_title[:150],
            "text": text_clean,
        })

    return extracted_pages


def chunk_extracted_pages(
    pages: List[Dict[str, Any]],
    chunk_size: int = 500,
    overlap: int = 50,
) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """Section-aware semantic chunking with exact provenance preservation."""
    chunks = []
    chunk_index = 0

    for page in pages:
        page_num = page["page_number"]
        section_title = page["section_title"]
        text = page["text"]

        start = 0
        while start < len(text):
            end = start + chunk_size
            chunk_text = text[start:end]

            if len(chunk_text.strip()) > 30:
                chunks.append({
                    "chunk_index": chunk_index,
                    "page_number": page_num,
                    "section_title": section_title,
                    "text": chunk_text.strip(),
                })
                chunk_index += 1

            start += (chunk_size - overlap)

    return chunks

A patient profile stores demographic and language information separately from authentication credentials. Password hashes are never presentation fields. Optional data should only be collected when required, and authorisation must restrict access to the appropriate patient or authorised healthcare worker. The actual backend fields must be distinguished from frontend-only sample fields; for example, patient_profiles does not define every village, allergy or health-note field used in a preview.

symptom_records stores its patient foreign key, input source, raw input reference, structured JSON data and report timestamp. The symptom service also creates a timeline event and can create an alert during analysis. JSONB supports structured narrative metadata while patient identity and ownership remain relational. Repeated analysis and alert duplication deserve explicit idempotency tests before deployment.

conversations stores patient ownership, language, status and start/end timestamps. conversation_messages stores sender type, text, optional metadata and creation time. The chat service filters supplied conversation IDs by patient ownership. Only recent turns are added to prompt context; they are not treated as authoritative medical evidence. Retention and deletion policies must address the sensitivity of conversation text.

MedGuide AI demonstrates a structured engineering approach to rural healthcare information access. Its web interface, application routes and backend modules bring together authentication, patient-owned records, deterministic matching, document provenance and retrieval-assisted generation. The two-laptop separation keeps frontend development independent from database and model infrastructure, while configurable service layers prepare integration.

The most important design decision is to place boundaries around generated healthcare content. Emergency paths bypass generative inference, unavailable embeddings fail closed, insufficient evidence produces refusal and responses can expose source metadata. These controls reduce specific engineering failure modes but do not eliminate hallucination, prove clinical safety or validate a diagnosis. Keyword rules, retrieval thresholds, multilingual handling and output validation need further expert review and systematic measurement.

The current evidence supports the claim of an implemented software prototype and tested frontend behaviours. It does not support reported clinical accuracy, quantified rural health outcomes, a fixed verified chunk count, complete offline operation or an already validated APK. Next steps are retrieval calibration, traceable rule review, secure API integration, measured language quality, improved evidence messaging and supervised usability studies. Speech, OCR and care-continuity enhancements should follow the approved scope and human review requirements.
